candidates.distinctConcept: Compare two powers of 2 with n in both exponents; determine first integer at which ordering crosses, keeping strict inequality distinct from equality.
candidates.taughtScope: TGS Autumn Index Laws broadly; strict algebraic inequalities and crossover reasoning not confirmed as specifically taught

replacement.stem: For each non-negative integer n, let A(n)=\frac{4^{n+3}\times8^{4-n}}{2^3} and B(n)=4^{n-2}\times2^5. What is the smallest n for which B(n)>A(n)?

options.wrongOperation: Incorrectly convert the 4 in A(n) as base 2, so A(n) is wrongly 2^(12−2n). Then 2n+1>12−2n gives 4n>11 and smallest n=3.
Correctly derive 3n>14 but round the threshold 14/3 down to n=4, instead of finding the first integer strictly greater than 14/3.
Omit the +1 when expanding B(n)=2^[2(n−2)+5], wrongly using 2^(2n). Then 2n>15−n gives n>5; answer 6.
Incorrectly convert 4^(n−2) as 2^(n−2) for B(n), so B(n)=2^(n+3). Then n+3>15−n gives n>6; answer 7.
Mistake 4 in A(n) for 8, so A(n) is wrongly constant 2^18. Compare B(n)=2^(2n+1) and require 2n+1>18; first n=9.

workedSolutionSteps: B(n)=2^{2(n-2)+5}=2^{2n+1}. Since the base 2 exceeds 1, B(n)>A(n) exactly when 2n+1>15-n.
Thus 3n>14, i.e. n>14/3. The smallest non-negative integer is n=5, option C.
At n=4, B=2^9<A=2^11; at n=5, B=2^11>A=2^10. This verifies the first crossover rather than an equality case.

candidates.distinctConcept: Reconstruct an integer parameter using product of HCF and LCM for two exponential integers; verify which one gives the minimum/maximum exponent.
candidates.taughtScope: Year 9 Autumn Index Laws heading is official; whether HCF/LCM-of-powers and parameter reconstruction were taught in the current class is unverified

replacement.stem: For an integer n with 3\le n\le19, define P(n)=\frac{4^{n+4}\times8^{5-n}}{2^4} and Q(n)=4^{n-3}. Both numbers are positive integers. Their highest common factor is 2^8 and their lowest common multiple is 2^{16}. Which value of n satisfies both facts?

options.wrongOperation: Use only P(n)=2^16 (assume P is the LCM), giving 19−n=16 and n=3, without verifying Q=1 and the incorrect HCF=1.
Use only Q(n)=2^8 (assume Q is the HCF), giving 2n−6=8 and n=7, but ignore that the LCM is 2^12, not 2^16.
Use HCF×LCM=PQ correctly, but wrongly expand the Q exponent 2(n−3) as 2n−4; then 19−n+2n−4=24 implies n=9.
Omit division by 2^4 in P(n), wrongly taking P=2^(23−n), then equate P to the HCF 2^8 and conclude n=15.
Convert 4^(n−3) incorrectly to 2^(n−3) rather than 2^[2(n−3)], equate Q to the LCM 2^16 and get n=19, ignoring HCF.

workedSolutionSteps: For two positive integers, HCF(P,Q)\times LCM(P,Q)=P Q. The given product is 2^{8+16}=2^{24}.
Check at n=11: P=2^8 and Q=2^{16}; the HCF is 2^8 and the LCM is 2^{16}. Therefore E is uniquely valid.
